1.goal: To open the lesson on the thing it is about: two documents that should agree, and do not.
1.interaction: T–S, one open question. Portuguese is fine at this point.
run: Ask her when she last had to read two documents against each other at work.
Take one answer and move on. The example does not have to be recent — it has to be concrete.
1.expected: One episode from her own work, named in a sentence or two.
1.support: If she describes reading one document carefully, bring it back to the pair — the work today is the comparison, not the reading.
1.challenge: Ask what she did with the mismatch once she found it: who she told, and in what order.
1.monitoring: Whether she reaches for a real episode or a generic one. The real one is what the briefing draws on later.
1.evidence: The example she gives — it is the situation the lesson keeps pointing back to.
1.transition: Move on when she has given one concrete example, real or invented.

2.goal: To establish who asked, what they asked for, and what she will leave the meeting with.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Give her time to read the brief.
Confirm two things out loud: the coordinator has read neither document, and the meeting is short.
2.expected: Recognition — this is the reading she already does at work, with someone waiting for the answer.
2.support: If the brief reads as one more text to study, ask what the coordinator will do with the answer. The purpose is what makes it short.
2.challenge: Ask what she would want to know before agreeing to brief someone who is going straight into another meeting.
2.monitoring: What the two documents disagree about is deliberately not said here. Do not fill it in; the first reading is where it arrives.
2.evidence: Whether she can state the task in one sentence without rereading the brief.
2.transition: Move on when she can say, in one sentence, what the coordinator needs from her.

3.goal: To get three hypotheses on the table so the first reading has a purpose.
3.interaction: T–S, three open questions. Hypotheses, not answers.
run: Read the three questions with her.
Collect one answer each and move on. Do not confirm or correct any of them — the documents are what test them.
3.expected: There is no right answer here. For your reference only, the usual territory: hours, assessment, who does what, what got cut.
3.support: If she answers about documents in general, ask her to answer about these two, in this school.
3.challenge: Ask which of her three guesses she would bet on, and what in her experience makes her say that.
3.monitoring: Whether she risks a guess at all, or waits to be told. What she predicts here is what she then reads for.
3.evidence: The three guesses, to hold against what the documents actually say in the next stage.
3.transition: Move on when three answers exist, however tentative.

4.goal: To read each document for what it IS, before comparing what they say.
4.interaction: S alone with both documents, then T–S.
run: Both documents, once, without notes.
Then the question on screen.
Keep her off the differences for now — if she jumps to them, say they are the next stage and write the point down for her.
4.expected: The plan is an instrument for one lesson, written by a teacher, changeable. The syllabus is a commitment across the course, written for people outside the classroom.
4.support: Ask who each document was written FOR. That question does most of the work.
4.challenge: Ask which of the two she would expect to be harder to change, and who would have to agree to it.
4.monitoring: Whether she reads for status or starts collecting differences. The order matters: what each document IS decides what a divergence means.
4.evidence: How she names the difference in status — that wording comes back in the briefing.
4.transition: Move on when she has named the difference in status between the two, in any words.

5.goal: To make her go back to the documents and point at the line, instead of answering from memory.
5.interaction: S alone on the six statements, then T–S on the ones she missed.
run: She opens the documents with the button and works through the six.
Then Check.
Take the wrong ones back to the line that decides them — read the line out, do not summarize it.
5.expected: 1 plan · 2 syllabus · 3 both · 4 plan · 5 syllabus · 6 neither.
5.support: If she answers from memory, close the answer and ask her to find the line first. The point of the stage is the line, not the verdict.
5.challenge: Ask which of the three real divergences the coordinator would have to settle first, and why that one.
5.monitoring: Number six is the one that matters. The listening task is only in the plan, and the syllabus says it does not list every task — so its silence is not disagreement. If she calls it a fourth difference, do not correct it as an error: it is the discovery of the next stage arriving early, and it is worth more than a right answer here.
5.evidence: Whether she returns to the document or answers from memory. This is the first isolated measure of reading for evidence.
5.transition: Move on when the three real divergences are named and located.

6.goal: For her to notice that three different things end up in the same sentence when she reports — and that only one of them is in the document.
6.interaction: S classifies on screen, then T–S discussion.
run: She classifies the six sentences, then Check.
Only after that, open the box with the question in it, and let her answer before revealing.
6.support: Ask: could someone with the document in front of them disagree with this sentence? If yes, it is not a quotation.
6.challenge: Ask her to turn the recommendation into an inference, and the inference into a quotation — and to say what she loses at each step.
6.monitoring: She is precise about this in Portuguese. What is missing is the English that marks the difference, not the distinction itself — so work on the wording, not on the concept.
6.evidence: Which of her own three findings she identifies as an inference. That is the one to listen for in the briefing.
6.transition: Move on when she can say which of her own three findings is an inference.

7.goal: To attach the source INSIDE the sentence, before the briefing runs.
7.interaction: S writes notes alone, then says each finding out loud to you.
run: She fills the three lines on the left — in note form, not sentences.
Then she says each of the three findings out loud, once, using one of the openings on the right.
Correct the position of the attribution, and nothing else, at this stage.
Keep the transcript closed until she has said all three: opened before, it stops being something to aim at and becomes a script to read.
exact: Rebuilding a late attribution: “Say that again, and start with where it comes from — The syllabus says…”
If the opening will not come: “Start with three words: According to the…”
7.expected: Any form where the source arrives with the claim, including forms that are not on the list.
7.support: If the source keeps arriving after the fact — It is 20 hours… that is in the syllabus — stop her and rebuild that one sentence with her, out loud, before going on.
7.challenge: Ask for the same three findings with the source at the END, then ask which version the coordinator could write down faster.
7.monitoring: Where the attribution lands. Early is the target; late is the habit being broken.
7.evidence: How many of the three carry the source inside the sentence — the number to compare with the briefing.
7.transition: Move on when three sentences have been said, with the source inside at least two of them.

8.goal: The production of the lesson. She briefs a coordinator who has read neither document, attributing each claim as she makes it.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are the coordinator; she is briefing you.
run: Let her run without interruption until she has given at least two findings.
Then interrupt ONCE, with one of the two lines below, word for word. Choose which one before the lesson.
Neither of them asks for information the documents do not contain.
exact: Sorry — which of the two is the one we promised the students?
Hold on. Is that in the document, or is that you reading it?
8.expected: Three findings, each attributed; the inference marked as one; a close that says what has to be decided.
8.support: The notes from the previous screen stay in view. They hold the structure, not the sentences — if she starts reading them out, take them away and ask her to say the last finding again.
8.challenge: After the briefing, ask for the whole thing again in ninety seconds, with the attributions kept.
8.monitoring: Where the attribution lands in the sentence, and whether the inference is still marked as one once she is under pressure.
8.evidence: One sentence of the briefing, written down word for word as she said it. It is the third field of the next screen.
8.transition: Move on when the three findings have been given and the interruption has been answered.

9.goal: Two points, taken from what she actually said, and one sentence rebuilt.
9.interaction: T–S, filling the four fields together, then a short retask.
run: Fill the board WITH her, not for her. One thing that worked, one to develop.
Put her own formulation in the third field, word for word as she said it, and build the fourth together.
Then Retask: the same finding once more, with the source inside the sentence.
9.expected: The point to develop is most likely the position of the attribution inside the sentence.
9.support: If nothing needs rebuilding — it happens — use the retask for the sentence she found hardest to say, not for a mistake.
9.challenge: Ask for the rebuilt sentence a second time, at the speed she would use in the real meeting.
9.monitoring: The board starts empty and stays hers. Do not pre-fill it with an error she did not make.
9.evidence: The two fields you fill here reach her Feedback tab — write them so she can act on them without you in front of her.
9.transition: Move on when the rebuilt sentence has been said out loud once.

10.goal: To register what was worked on, and how she felt doing it.
10.interaction: S ticks the list and answers the scale; T–S on the closing question.
run: She reads the list and ticks what she recognizes.
The scale is her perception, not your assessment — do not argue with it.
Say the homework out loud and do not put it on screen: the post-class is there if she wants it, and nothing in it is required for lesson 2.
10.expected: Some of the lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence scale.
10.support: If she ticks nothing, read the list with her and ask which line she could use at work tomorrow.
10.challenge: Ask which of today's phrases she would use first in the meeting she actually has this week.
10.monitoring: A low mark on the third line after a briefing that went well is worth noting: it is the gap between doing and knowing that she did.
10.evidence: Her own confidence reading, against what you saw in the briefing. Fill the post-lesson record before you close.
